title: The One Crossing: the Exile's Daughter, Highgate Hill, and the Road That Winds Up-Hill All the Way
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: 38 Charlotte Street, Marylebone: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'). The house is renumbered into Hallam Street, but Wikipedia's Christina article gives 110 and its Dante Gabriel article gives 105; the disagreement is unresolved, so no number is asserted. Coordinate from OSM at the commemorated site.
stops.campa: Frances Polidori bears her fourth child in four years and names her Christina Georgina. The father is Gabriele Rossetti of Vasto, poet, driven out of the Kingdom of Naples for his politics and living now by teaching Italian to English pupils in a rented London house. The mother is a Polidori, sister to the John Polidori who attended Byron and wrote The Vampyre. Dante Gabriel was born in this same room two years earlier, William Michael the year after him, Maria Francesca the year before. The table speaks Italian; the street outside speaks English.
suggested_refs: The stone plaque marking the Rossetti birthplace in Hallam Street, Marylebone

stops.name: 166 Albany Street, Regent's Park: the long address
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the family's residence here c. 1836-1853 rests on W. M. Rossetti's Some Reminiscences (1906) and Jan Marsh's 1994 biography, neither reachable in full text this pass. Coordinate corrected from OSM; the gathered longitude sat about 150 m west of the street.
stops.campa: The household settles on the eastern edge of Regent's Park and stays some seventeen years, the longest address of Christina's childhood. Italian exiles come and go through the front room; her father's teaching income is unreliable and the family knows it. Her brothers are sent out to school. Christina and Maria are taught at home, chiefly by their mother, out of fairy tales, devotional books and Romantic poetry. She reads more than she is taught, and she begins, at eleven or twelve, to write verses of her own.
suggested_refs: W. M. Rossetti, Some Reminiscences (1906), on the Albany Street household
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Holmer Green, Buckinghamshire: the grandfather's cottage
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the childhood summers here come from W. M. Rossetti (1906), not reverified this pass. The year is representative of a run of summers, not a dated visit. Coordinate corrected from OSM; the gathered pair fell about 6 km east, near Amersham.
stops.campa: The children are sent out of London in summer to Gaetano Polidori's cottage in the Chiltern country. Here the exile's daughter learns the only landscape she will ever write from first hand: hedgerows, cornfields, small birds, a garden with a wall around it. The Italy her father lost is a language spoken indoors and a grief carried at the table. The fields at Holmer Green are what her nursery rhymes and her nature verse are made of, and she will use them for sixty years without ever calling them English.
suggested_refs: Gaetano Polidori's cottage at Holmer Green, the family's summer refuge

stops.name: Christ Church, Albany Street: the Tractarian parish
stops.date_confidence: the church is attested (consecrated 13 July 1837, Oxford Movement, first vicar William Dodsworth) and her worship here is attested; the depth of its formative effect is Marsh's reading and is a reconstruction. Coordinate from Wikipedia's own figure, about 200 m north of the gathered pair.
stops.campa: Five years old at its consecration, the church is as new as she is. Its clergy are Puseyites and its year runs on a strict calendar of fasts and feasts. The sacraments there are handled as though they were dangerous, and Christina takes all of it. The first vicar, William Dodsworth, will go over to Rome; she never will, and the line she draws between High Anglican devotion and Roman obedience is the line on which she later breaks an engagement. Her poems keep this parish's calendar long after she stops being able to walk to it.
suggested_refs: Christ Church, Albany Street, consecrated 1837, a founding parish of the Oxford Movement in London
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: London, the grandfather's press prints Verses
stops.date_confidence: attested for both facts, which the gathered pool had conflated: Poets.org dates her first poems to 1842, Wikipedia dates Gaetano Polidori's printing of the Verses to 1847. The press's address is not established in any reachable source, so the stop takes the generic London pin.
stops.campa: Her grandfather keeps a printing press at home and in 1847 sets her poems in type. The result is a small volume called Verses, with no publisher and no price on it. She is sixteen. Two years before, at about fifteen, she had broken down, left off lessons and turned hard toward religion; the years between are illness and prayer. The book is the first printed thing carrying her writing, and it exists because a family that lost a country kept a press in the parlour.
suggested_refs: Verses (1847), privately printed by Gaetano Polidori

stops.name: Gower Street, the Brotherhood is named
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate inherited byte-identical from working/journeys/william_holman_hunt.journey.json. The month within 1848 is conventional.
stops.campa: In the Millais family house seven young men give themselves a name and a set of initials: the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. Two of them are Christina's brothers, Dante Gabriel and William Michael. William Holman Hunt is a third; John Everett Millais is at home. Christina is seventeen and not in the room, because no woman is. She will supply the Brotherhood its first published poems, and within a year her face is on its first Virgin. Neither service is signed with her name.
suggested_refs: The Millais family house on Gower Street, where the PRB took its name in 1848

stops.name: London, the engagement to James Collinson
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the engagement (Wikipedia); the month is not established. Two of her poems appear in The Athenaeum the same year, her first print outside the family.
stops.campa: James Collinson, painter, founding member of the Brotherhood, asks for her and is accepted. He had been a Roman Catholic and had come over to the Church of England to be eligible; she takes him on that footing. Her brother William Michael thinks little of the match and says so at the time. The same year two of her poems appear in The Athenaeum, the first of her work to reach a public that is not related to her. She is eighteen, engaged, and in print, and the arrangement holds less than two years.
stops.quote: My heart is like a singing bird / Whose nest is in a watered shoot; / My heart is like an appletree / Whose boughs are bent with thick-set fruit;
stops.quote_source: A Birthday, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Athenaeum, 1848, carrying her first non-family publication

stops.name: Charlotte Street, sitting as the Virgin
stops.date_confidence: the sitting and the picture are attested (Wikipedia); the working address is a reconstruction, pinned to the family's Charlotte Street district rather than to a studio the sources do not name.
stops.campa: Her brother paints The Girlhood of Mary Virgin and puts her face on the mother of God. It is among the first pictures shown with the initials PRB after the signature, and the Virgin in it is nineteen years old and lives at home. The Brotherhood's programme is to paint from the model rather than from the manner of the schools; the model available in that house is his sister. She sits, and the movement's founding image of holiness is a portrait of a woman who is at that moment engaged to one of its members.
suggested_refs: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, The Girlhood of Mary Virgin (1848-49), Tate

stops.name: London, seven poems as Ellen Alleyne
stops.date_confidence: attested: The Germ ran four issues, January to April or May 1850, printed by Tupper and Sons, edited by William Michael Rossetti, and sold badly. The count of seven poems is Poets.org and W. M. Rossetti's own 1901 facsimile reprint. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from working/journeys/william_holman_hunt.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Brotherhood starts a magazine, Thoughts towards Nature in Art and Literature, conducted principally by Artists. It runs four issues and dies of poor sales. Christina contributes seven poems under a name her brother William Michael picks for her: Ellen Alleyne. The men sign themselves. She does not. The magazine is the movement's manifesto, and the one contributor its readers cannot identify is a woman writing under a name her editor invented, who is also her brother.
suggested_refs: The Germ, four issues, 1850; W. M. Rossetti's facsimile reprint of 1901

stops.name: Regent Street, Ecce Ancilla Domini exhibited
stops.date_confidence: attested: the picture is dated 1850 and first exhibited April 1850 at the Old Portland Gallery, Regent Street, though it is conventionally catalogued 1849-50. The gallery's exact position on the street is not established; the stop is pinned to Regent Street.
stops.campa: She sits for her brother a second time and he hangs the result on Regent Street: the Annunciation, the angel standing, the girl pulled back on the bed against the wall in a white shift, not adoring but afraid. Critics are savage about the whole Pre-Raphaelite exhibition that season. Christina's face is now twice public property, as the child Mary and as the startled one, in a movement whose theory of truth to nature has been satisfied, in both cases, by asking a member of the family.
suggested_refs: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Ecce Ancilla Domini! (1849-50), first exhibited Old Portland Gallery, April 1850

stops.name: Christ Church, Albany Street: the engagement broken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the direction: Wikipedia states she ended the engagement in 1850 when Collinson reverted to Catholicism. The gathered chronology had Collinson breaking it, which is backwards; that error is recorded in the report. Month not established.
stops.campa: Collinson goes back to Rome. Christina ends the engagement. He resigns from the Brotherhood, tries the priesthood at a Jesuit college and never finishes the training; he marries someone else and paints on for thirty years. She does not marry at all. The doctrine she was raised in at this church, that the English communion is catholic and need not go to Rome to be so, has just cost her a husband, and she will pay the same price again sixteen years later for the same reason from the opposite direction.
suggested_refs: Christ Church, Albany Street, the parish whose churchmanship decided the match

stops.name: Fromefield, Frome: the day school
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia): in 1853 she helped her mother run a school at Fromefield, Frome. Coordinate corrected from OSM; the gathered pair sat about 900 m north of the locality.
stops.campa: Her father can no longer teach and the money is gone. Christina and her mother open a day school in a Somerset town and try to live off it. It fails inside the year. She is twenty-two, keeping a schoolroom two days' travel from everyone she knows, in the softest country in England, and what she writes about the place is not complaint. Nearly a century and a half later a stone will be set in Frome with her lines cut into it, and the town will claim the failed schoolmistress as its own.
stops.quote: an abundance of green slopes and gentle declivities: no boldness or grandeur but plenty of peaceful beauty
stops.quote_source: Christina Rossetti on Frome, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'
suggested_refs: The Fromefield day school kept by Frances and Christina Rossetti, 1853-54

stops.name: London, Gabriele Rossetti dies
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Gabriele Rossetti'), aged 71. The family's return from Frome and Christina's nursing duties are reconstruction from W. M. Rossetti (1906).
stops.campa: The exile dies in London, seventy-one years old, having spent more of his life in England than in Italy and never having gone back. He is buried in Highgate. The school at Frome closes and the women come home. Christina takes up the work that will occupy the next forty years alongside the writing: nursing the sick of her own household, first her father, then her mother, then her aunts, then a man who wanted to marry her, then herself. She is twenty-three.
suggested_refs: Gabriele Rossetti's grave in the family plot, Highgate Cemetery West

stops.name: Hastings, the sea air
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Jan Marsh, 1994, not reverified this pass). The year stands for a pattern of repeated 1850s visits rather than a dated stay.
stops.campa: The family retreats to the Channel coast for her health, and keeps retreating there. Sea air is what Victorian medicine offers a young woman who is tired and unwell without a name for the trouble. The pattern set at Hastings holds for life: when Christina Rossetti is ill she goes south to an English shore, not across water. She will leave England exactly twice, and she will spend far more of her days looking at the sea from this side of it than from any other place outside London.
suggested_refs: The Rossetti family's recurring convalescent lodgings on the Sussex coast
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

segments.name: Highgate Hill and the Goblin Fruit

stops.name: St Mary Magdalene Penitentiary, Highgate Hill: the fallen women
stops.date_confidence: attested for the volunteering and its rough decade-long span, and for the composition of Goblin Market in spring 1859 shortly before it began (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'; Wikipedia, 'Goblin Market'). The causal link between the institution and the poem is interpretation, not attestation.
stops.campa: She begins volunteering at the London Diocesan Penitentiary on Highgate Hill, an Anglican house for women taken off the streets, run on silence and penance. She keeps at it for about ten years. That same spring she writes a poem about two sisters, one of whom eats forbidden fruit from men who are not men and wastes toward death, and the other of whom goes to the goblins, refuses to eat, and carries the juice home on her face to save her. The refuge stands a few hundred yards from the grave she will be put in.
stops.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
stops.quote_source: Goblin Market, closing lines, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The St Mary Magdalene diocesan penitentiary, Highgate Hill

stops.name: Red Lion Square, the Firm is founded
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate inherited byte-identical from working/journeys/william_holman_hunt.journey.json. Christina is not a partner and no source places her at the founding; the stop marks the circle her brother is at the centre of.
stops.campa: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Company opens for business with Dante Gabriel Rossetti as a partner, alongside William Morris, Edward Burne-Jones, Ford Madox Brown, Philip Webb and Peter Paul Marshall. William Holman Hunt is not among them. It is the same square where Morris and Burne-Jones had taken rooms, and where Rossetti told Morris that a man should paint rather than build. Christina is no part of the enterprise and keeps her distance from it; the poem that will make her name is written already, two years old and still unpublished.
suggested_refs: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co., founded 1861 at Red Lion Square

stops.name: London, Goblin Market and Other Poems
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'; Wikipedia, 'Goblin Market'): Macmillan and Co., 1862, illustrated by Dante Gabriel Rossetti. Macmillan's exact London premises are not asserted here; the stop takes the generic London pin.
stops.campa: Macmillan brings out her first commercial book, with her brother's illustrations at the front. It makes her, at thirty-one, one of the two or three poets in England anybody argues about. The title poem is read as a children's rhyme, as a temperance tract, as a Eucharist, as a fable of the penitentiary, and later as a coded account of desire between women, of addiction, and of Christian England looking at strangers and calling them goblins. She says it is a fairy tale. The arguing has not stopped.
stops.quote: Morning and evening / Maids heard the goblins cry: / "Come buy our orchard fruits, / Come buy, come buy: / Apples and quinces, / Lemons and oranges, / Plump unpecked cherries, / Melons and raspberries, / Bloom-down-cheeked peaches, / Swart-headed mulberries,"
stops.quote_source: Goblin Market, opening lines, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: Goblin Market and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1862, with two designs by Dante Gabriel Rossetti

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, Chelsea: visiting her brother
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994; W. M. Rossetti 1906) for Christina's visits; the move after Elizabeth Siddal's death in 1862 is attested. Coordinate corrected from OSM, where the house is tagged for Rossetti and Swinburne; the gathered pair sat about 420 m west.
stops.campa: Widowed, Dante Gabriel takes a riverside house in Chelsea and fills it with peacocks, wombats, armadillos and a rotating population of poets. Swinburne lodges there. Jane Morris, whom he found at the Oxford theatre and painted as Guenevere, comes and sits and stays; she is another man's wife and the arrangement will end with a joint lease on a manor house in Oxfordshire. Christina visits her brother in this house, disapproving of almost everything in it and defending him to everyone outside it.
suggested_refs: 16 Cheyne Walk, Queen's House, Dante Gabriel Rossetti's home from 1862
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Paris, the road south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994; W. M. Rossetti's diaries as relayed in the secondary literature). A shorter Paris excursion in 1861 is claimed by the same source. The atlas interlock pass found no direct evidence that Christina Rossetti visited Paris at all, and notes that this coordinate is already William Holman Hunt's pin; both readings are carried, unreconciled. Coordinate inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: She crosses the Channel with her mother and William Michael and turns south through France. She had been to Paris once before, briefly, four years earlier; this time the destination is Italy, the country her father was thrown out of and she has never seen. She is thirty-four. The whole of the travelling she will ever do is in front of her and will be finished by autumn. William Holman Hunt has stood in this same city, and will stand in Jerusalem; Christina goes no further than the Lombard plain.
suggested_refs: W. M. Rossetti's travel diaries of the 1865 Continental tour
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Lucerne, under the Rigi
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994, not reverified this pass); the month is inferred from the tour's sequence, not attested.
stops.campa: The party halts on the lake shore before the climb into the Alps. The scenery in her letters turns extraordinary and the writer of them does not. She reports herself homesick and anxious in the middle of the finest view in Europe. The mountains get a line each in her letters; the post from home gets paragraphs. She is not a bad traveller so much as a woman who already knows what she is for and where she does it, and who has come the length of two countries to confirm that the place is a room in London with her family in it.
suggested_refs: Christina Rossetti's letters from the 1865 tour, quoted in the biographical literature
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Splugen Pass, the crossing into Italy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the route detail is explicitly treated as unverified in the research pool, and the day is an ordering device rather than a claim.
stops.campa: The road climbs the Alps and drops over the watershed, and Christina Rossetti enters Italy. It is the only time in her life. She is Italian on her father's side, was raised bilingual, has written in the language, and has spent thirty-four years hearing about a country as a thing that was taken away. The pass is a hard road and it is short. The border it crosses is the one her whole family has been standing on the wrong side of since before she was born.
stops.quote: Does the road wind up-hill all the way? / Yes, to the very end. / Will the day's journey take the whole long day? / From morn to night, my friend.
stops.quote_source: Up-Hill, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Splugen Pass road between Graubunden and Lombardy
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Lake Como, the first sight of Italy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994); the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Below the pass the water opens out and the country her father lost begins. She looks at it as a foreigner who is not one. Everything on this shore is exactly as it was described to her at a London table by a man teaching Italian to English children for money because he could not go home. The description was accurate. She has a few weeks in the country and then she will go back to England and stay there for the remaining twenty-nine years of her life.
suggested_refs: The Lombard lakes, the first Italian ground Christina Rossetti stood on
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Milan, the Duomo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994); the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The tour reaches Milan and its cathedral, a forest of marble put up over four and a half centuries. She goes in. The Anglo-Catholic devotion she learned at Christ Church, Albany Street, was an English reconstruction of what this building simply is, and she has arrived at the original as a visitor. Her Italian, learned at her father's knee at the same time as English, works here for the first and only time on the ground it was made for, and she uses it to buy things and ask directions.
suggested_refs: The Duomo of Milan, visited on the 1865 tour
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Verona, the furthest east
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; her admiration for Verona is referenced in the secondary literature from letters not independently reverified this pass.
stops.campa: She writes warmly of Verona, a city she knows through Shakespeare before she knows it through her father. The Italy she is moving across is doubly borrowed: an English poet's stage set laid over an exile's memory, with the actual streets underneath both. She is near the far end of her travelling now. Everything east and south of here, Venice, Florence, Rome, the Abruzzo coast where her father was born, remains a name in a language she speaks and a place she will not see.
suggested_refs: Christina Rossetti's letters on Verona, 1865
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Bologna, the turn north
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994). The reason for turning back is disputed in the secondary literature: ill health, homesickness, or simply the planned itinerary. The dispute is left open here.
stops.campa: At Bologna the party turns round and starts for home through Switzerland and France. Why is not agreed: her health, her nerves, or a route that always ended here. She is four hundred miles short of Rome and two hundred short of the Adriatic town her father was born in. She never comes back. The imagery of this summer comes back in her later work, in poems about a country that is wanted and not reached; readers have taken that country for heaven, and the sources do not say what she meant by it.
suggested_refs: The southernmost point of the 1865 Rossetti tour
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Vasto, Abruzzo: the town she does not reach
stops.date_confidence: NOT A PERSONAL STOP. Christina Rossetti is not attested, and is not traditionally claimed, to have visited Vasto. The pin is ancestral context only: her father's birthplace, marked at the moment the 1865 tour turned north without going there. Flagged so it is never read as travel.
stops.campa: Two hundred miles south of where the carriages turn, on the Adriatic, is the town Gabriele Rossetti was born in and left for Malta and then London, carrying a price on his politics. His daughter comes within a week's travel of it in the only summer she is ever on this peninsula, and does not go. Vasto stays what it has always been in that family, a place spoken of in the past tense at an English table. The exile is complete in the second generation, and it is completed by a decision nobody records.
suggested_refs: Vasto, Abruzzo, birthplace of Gabriele Rossetti

segments.name: The Illness and the Closing House

stops.name: London, Charles Bagot Cayley's proposal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the involvement from about 1864, the proposal and the refusal on religious grounds (Wikipedia); the nursing of him in his last illness is reconstruction from Marsh. The Prince's Progress and Other Poems is published by Macmillan the same year.
stops.campa: The scholar and translator Charles Bagot Cayley asks her to marry him. He is an agnostic. She refuses him for it, exactly as she refused Collinson sixteen years earlier for believing too much, and then keeps him as the closest friend of her life and nurses him at the end of it. The Prince's Progress and Other Poems comes out from Macmillan the same year, illustrated again by her brother: a poem about a bridegroom who dawdles on the road and arrives to find the bride dead.
stops.quote: Because the birthday of my life / Is come, my love is come to me.
stops.quote_source: A Birthday, closing couplet, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1866
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: 56 Euston Square, the household moves
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Marsh 1994, not reverified this pass); the address later becomes Endsleigh Gardens. The year within the late 1860s is approximate.
stops.campa: William Michael's salary at the Inland Revenue steadies the family and they move again. Christina is thirty-six and her health is turning. From here the shape of her working life is fixed: a woman who does not go out much, writing in a room, sending manuscripts to Macmillan, receiving visitors, keeping the fasts. She has already done all her travelling. The rest of the journey is between an upstairs room and a church, and it will produce most of her devotional prose.
suggested_refs: 56 Euston Square, later Endsleigh Gardens, the Rossetti household of the late 1860s
sources: Jan Marsh, Christina Rossetti: A Literary Biography (1994)

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery, the coffin opened
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exhumation and its purpose (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'; documented across the Rossetti literature). The graveside embellishments that circulate with it, Siddal's hair reported still growing and Howell's exact words, are legend and are not repeated here.
stops.campa: Seven years after burying his wife with the only manuscript of his poems in her coffin, Dante Gabriel wants the poems back. Permission is obtained, the family grave at Highgate is opened by night, and Elizabeth Siddal's coffin is lifted so the book can be taken out of it. The grave is the Rossetti grave. Gabriele is already in it. Christina and her mother will go into it in their turn, into ground that has been dug up once already for the sake of a volume of verse.
suggested_refs: The Rossetti family grave, Highgate Cemetery West, opened October 1869

stops.name: London, Graves' disease
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1872 (Wikipedia). The geography lens gave 1871 and is overruled by the article; that discrepancy is recorded in the report. Month not established. Sing-Song, illustrated by Arthur Hughes, is published by Routledge the same year.
stops.campa: Exophthalmic goitre, near fatal in the attack that reveals it. It swells her eyes and her throat, alters her face permanently, and never leaves. She is forty-one. In the same year Routledge publishes Sing-Song, a nursery rhyme book with Arthur Hughes's drawings, the gentlest thing she ever made. From here she withdraws from company by degrees, and not from writing. The visiting stops, then the walking out; the work at the desk does not stop for another twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book, Routledge, 1872, illustrated by Arthur Hughes

stops.name: London, Maria enters the Society of All Saints
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Maria Francesca Rossetti'): she entered the Anglican Society of All Saints, the All Saints Sisters of the Poor, in 1874 at age 46. Month not established.
stops.campa: Her elder sister Maria Francesca takes the habit at forty-six and enters the Society of All Saints, the All Saints Sisters of the Poor. The Oxford Movement had restored religious sisterhood to the English church within their own lifetime and against loud opposition; Maria walks into it. Christina, who has spent ten years serving in a penitentiary run by exactly such women, stays outside the wall. She is forty-three, she keeps the fasts at home, and she stays in the house with their mother.
suggested_refs: The All Saints Sisters of the Poor, the Anglican order Maria Francesca Rossetti entered in 1874

stops.name: 30 Torrington Square, Bloomsbury: the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence, the stone tablet on the facade and the death here (Wikipedia); the span 1876-1894 is not in the cited source and is a reconstruction. Coordinate corrected from OSM; the gathered pair fell nearer Russell Square, and the afterlife lens's slightly different pin is harmonised to this one.
stops.campa: She moves into the house she will die in, with her mother and two aunts, and takes charge of all three. The house is Bloomsbury brick, and the tablet that names her goes onto the front long afterward. Almost everything else she writes is written here: the devotional prose, the commentaries, the late poems. The woman who crossed the Alps once at thirty-four spends her last eighteen years within a few streets, nursing the old women of her family one after another until the house is empty except for her.
stops.quote: TO MY MOTHER, IN ALL REVERENCE AND LOVE, I INSCRIBE THIS BOOK
stops.quote_source: Dedication, Goblin Market and Other Poems, 1906 Boston edition (Little, Brown and Company), Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: 30 Torrington Square, Bloomsbury, with its commemorative tablet

stops.name: Brompton Cemetery, Maria's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Maria Francesca Rossetti'): died of ovarian cancer aged 49, buried in the convent plot at Brompton Cemetery.
stops.campa: Maria dies of ovarian cancer at forty-nine, two years into the religious life, and is buried not in the family grave at Highgate but in her order's plot at Brompton, on the other side of London. It is the first of the family deaths Christina has to survive without having nursed it. The Rossetti dead are now in two cemeteries, and Christina is the one keeping the account of both. Her mother is seventy-six and there are two aunts in the house as well.
suggested_refs: The All Saints Sisters' plot, Brompton Cemetery

stops.name: 30 Torrington Square, the devotional prose
stops.date_confidence: attested (Poets.org): Seek and Find, 1879; A Pageant and Other Poems and Called to Be Saints, both 1881. The address of composition is a reconstruction consistent with her known residence.
stops.campa: Seek and Find in 1879, then in one year, 1881, both A Pageant and Other Poems and Called to Be Saints. She is forty-eight when the first of them appears. The public still wants the poet of Goblin Market and she is writing commentary on scripture. Reviewers then and critics since have called this a waste of a talent. She goes on with it for the rest of her life, and the verse keeps appearing inside the prose, set into the argument wherever the argument runs out of words.
suggested_refs: Seek and Find (1879); Called to Be Saints (1881); A Pageant and Other Poems (1881)

stops.name: Birchington-on-Sea, Kent: Dante Gabriel dies
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti'): died 9 April 1882, Easter Sunday, aged 53, of Bright's disease at Westcliff Bungalow. The gathered date of 10 April is off by one day and is corrected here. Coordinate matches OSM Birchington-on-Sea.
stops.campa: Her brother dies of Bright's disease on Easter Sunday, in a rented bungalow on the Kent coast, fifty-three years old. He is buried in the churchyard there and not at Highgate, so the family grave that was opened for his wife's manuscript does not take him. William Holman Hunt, who was in the room on Gower Street when the seven of them chose the name, outlives him by twenty-eight years and dies last of the founders. Christina has twelve years left and writes them in Bloomsbury.
suggested_refs: Westcliff Bungalow, Birchington-on-Sea, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti's grave in the churchyard

stops.name: 30 Torrington Square, The Face of the Deep
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; Poets.org) for the publication in 1892. The composition address is a reconstruction consistent with her residence.
stops.campa: She publishes a devotional commentary on the Book of Revelation, several hundred pages of it, working verse by verse through the apocalypse with poems set into the prose wherever the prose runs out. It is the longest thing she ever wrote and the least read. The woman who is remembered for a nursery rhyme about goblins spends the end of her working life on the beasts, the seals, the woman clothed with the sun, and the city that comes down out of heaven.
suggested_refs: The Face of the Deep: A Devotional Commentary on the Apocalypse (1892)

stops.name: 30 Torrington Square, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; Poets.org). Breast cancer was diagnosed in 1893, a tumor removed, and the cancer had recurred by September of that year; an enlarged Sing-Song also appeared in 1893, on weaker sourcing.
stops.campa: Breast cancer is found in 1893, the tumour is cut out, and it comes back within months. She dies in the house two days before the end of the year, sixty-four years old. Her mother, her sister, her father and her most famous brother have all gone before her; William Michael, the youngest of the boys, is left to bury her and then to edit her. The last of the Rossetti generation born in Charlotte Street to an exile who taught Italian for a living dies in Bloomsbury, less than a mile from where she started.
stops.quote: Remember me when I am gone away, / Gone far away into the silent land; / When you can no more hold me by the hand, / Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
stops.quote_source: Remember, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: 30 Torrington Square, where Christina Rossetti died, 29 December 1894

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery, the family grave
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti'; Wikipedia, 'Highgate Cemetery') for the burial in the family grave on the west side with her father, her mother and Elizabeth Siddal. William Michael joins them in 1919 and the ashes of four further family members follow.
stops.campa: She goes into the ground on the west side of Highgate, with Gabriele, with Frances, and with Elizabeth Siddal, whose coffin this same family opened twenty-six years before. The burial is on the second of January, 1895. William Michael follows in 1919 and four more sets of ashes after him. A few hundred yards down the hill stands the penitentiary where she gave ten years to women nobody else would house. The grave and the refuge are on the same hill, and she spent years in both.
stops.quote: Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.
stops.quote_source: Remember, closing couplet, in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Rossetti family grave, Highgate Cemetery West

stops.name: London, William Michael's collected edition
stops.date_confidence: attested that her brother edited and published the collected poetical works with a memoir in 1904 (Poets.org); the full bibliographic description, Macmillan, The Poetical Works of Christina Georgina Rossetti, comes from the bibliographic record rather than a source fetched this pass.
stops.campa: Ten years after her death her surviving brother brings out the collected poems with his own memoir at the front, and that memoir is how England reads her for the next seventy years: the shy invalid, the saintly spinster, the sister of the painter. He named her Ellen Alleyne in 1850 and he names her again in 1904. She had written, in a preface to her own book, that it would speak for itself or not at all. The edition that carries her into the twentieth century speaks for her throughout.
stops.quote: My little book seems scarcely to admit of prefatory words: either it will speak for itself, or all my additions must fail to speak for it.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the American edition, Goblin Market and Other Poems, 1906 Boston edition (Little, Brown and Company), Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: W. M. Rossetti (ed.), The Poetical Works of Christina Georgina Rossetti, Macmillan, 1904

stops.name: King's College Chapel, Cambridge: In the Bleak Midwinter
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'In the Bleak Midwinter'): the poem first appeared in Scribner's Monthly, January 1872; Holst's tune Cranham dates from 1906 in The English Hymnal, Darke's setting from 1909, and Darke's is the version broadcast from King's. The 2008 poll of choirmasters and choral experts is attested. The chapel pin marks the broadcast tradition, not a Rossetti visit.
stops.campa: A poem she published in an American magazine in 1872 is set by Gustav Holst to a tune called Cranham for The English Hymnal, and again by Harold Darke three years later. Darke's version is what the choir at King's sings, and what the wireless carries out of this chapel every Christmas Eve to a country that mostly cannot name the author. In 2008 British choirmasters vote it the best Christmas carol there is. She has been dead twelve years when the first of the two tunes is written.
stops.quote: In the bleak mid-winter / Frosty wind made moan,
stops.quote_source: A Christmas Carol, Wikisource, better known as In the Bleak Midwinter
suggested_refs: The Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols, King's College Chapel, Cambridge

stops.name: Baton Rouge, Louisiana: the Complete Poems
stops.date_confidence: attested that Louisiana State University Press published the three-volume Complete Poems between 1979 and 1990, volume one in 1979 (Poets.org). The gathered claim compressed this into a single 1979 date. Poets.org does not name Rebecca W. Crump as editor; that attribution comes from the bibliographic record and is a reconstruction here.
stops.campa: A university press on the Mississippi begins issuing the three volumes that finally put every surviving poem in order, with the variants, the datings and the retentions she made herself. It takes eleven years to complete. From the late 1970s the rereading starts in earnest: Goblin Market as coded desire between women, as an addiction narrative, as a Christian text that makes strangers into goblins. The poem specifies none of it. The arguments are built on the poem and cannot be put to the woman who wrote it.
stops.quote: I retain this little poem, not as historically accurate, but as written and published before I heard the supposed facts of its first verse contradicted.
stops.quote_source: Author's note to 'In the Round Tower at Jhansi', Goblin Market and Other Poems, 1906 Boston edition, Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: The Complete Poems of Christina Rossetti, 3 vols., Louisiana State University Press, 1979-1990

stops.name: Frome, Somerset: the poetry stone
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia) that a millennium project in 2000 set an inscribed stone in the former grounds of North Hill House, Frome. The coordinate is Frome town centre; the stone's exact position within the former grounds is not established in any reachable source.
stops.campa: A hundred and forty-seven years after her mother's school failed here, the town cuts three of her lines into a stone and sets it in the grounds of a vanished house for the millennium. She had been in Frome about a year, in the worst season of the family's money, doing work she was not good at. The place kept her anyway. The marks left on English ground are a tablet in Bloomsbury where she died, a grave on Highgate hill, and a stone in a Somerset garden where she once failed to run a school.
stops.quote: Love lights the sun: love through the dark / Lights the moon's evanescent arc: / Same Love lights up the glow-worm's spark.
stops.quote_source: What Good Shall My Life Do Me, inscribed on the Frome millennium poetry stone (Wikipedia, 'Christina Rossetti')
suggested_refs: The millennium poetry stone in the former grounds of North Hill House, Frome

stops.name: Christ Church, Albany Street: the day in the calendar
stops.date_confidence: the day, 27 April, is attested (Wikipedia); the YEAR IS A PLACEHOLDER. No reachable source gives the year Christina Rossetti entered the Church of England's calendar, and the year here is set to match the Frome memorial purely to order the stop. Only the day is a claim.
stops.campa: The church that formed her, Tractarian, five years older than her first poems, belongs to a communion that now keeps her name in its calendar on the twenty-seventh of April. She is commemorated as a poet by the body whose fasts and feasts she wrote inside for fifty years, and whose boundary with Rome cost her both the men who asked her. Elsewhere she is a carol, a nursery rhyme, a title lifted for a crime novel, and a poem argued over in universities. Here she is simply a day.
suggested_refs: The Church of England's calendar entry for Christina Rossetti, 27 April
